title: When Do Discrete Actions Make Good Continuous Controllers?

paper.title: When Do Discrete Actions Make Good Continuous Controllers?
paper.abstract:
Abstract Though modern AI models like LLMs predict discrete tokens, today’s robotic foundation models represent actions as continuous vectors. In this paper, we challenge this common consensus by asking if continuous action parametrizations are superior to their discrete counterparts. We conduct an extensive comparison of single-step regression and multi-step flow variants of both continuous and discrete policies in both from-scratch single-task and multi-task VLA training, in both simulation and on real hardware. In all regimes, we
find that discrete action prediction, even the most naive, uniform-bin quantization, can match or even outperform continuous-action policies in task success rate. Moreover, we find that the challenge to discrete action policies is not action precision, but rather factorization error introduced by product-distribution predictions across time and action dimensions. We show that, when paired with the correct interventions—iterative computation through discrete flows, or distribution sharpening through classifier-free guidance—discrete flow policies can turn this weakness into a strength, enabling more responsive action changes during a predicted action chunk. Lastly, we show that attempts to explicitly inject geometric information into discrete policies, e.g. through corruption processes that emulate continuous flow matching, do not yield consistent improvements. Taken together, our findings question existing assumptions that robotic action prediction requires distinct design decisions compared to other AI domains, and motivates the possibility of discrete action prediction as a compelling alternative to today’s continuous action parametrizations. sections.heading: 1 Introduction
sections.text: A major goal of modern robot learning is to perform complex and varied tasks to high precision. As a result, the community has devoted significant study to the question of how to parametrize the actions predicted by robotic policies and foundation models, such as vision-language-action models (VLAs) ( Brohan et al., 2023 ; Kim et al., 2024 ; Black et al., 2025 ; NVIDIA et al., 2025 ) and world action models (WAMs) ( Li et al., 2025 ; Ye et al., 2026b ; Kim et al., 2026 ; Li et al., 2026b ) . The common consensus is that robot models should predict continuous-valued actions during deployment, as these are lossless and therefore support high-precision behavior. For example, most of today’s VLAs predict actions using continuous-space generative models, such as flow ( Black et al., 2025 ; Physical Intelligence and others, 2025 ) or diffusion models ( Chi et al., 2023 ) , which are believed to better capture training data diversity whilst enhancing the precision of action predictions. At the same time, modern robot learning is adopting increasingly more features from other AI domains, notably language modeling. These include test-time reasoning ( Wei et al., 2022 ) , on-task self-correction ( Huang et al., 2022 ) , future goal prediction ( Du et al., 2023 ) , and long-term memory ( Wang et al., 2023 ) . In fact, recent work has showcased the possibility that frontier language models can directly control robot embodiments through text generation ( Brohan et al., 2023 ; Kim et al., 2024 ) . Yet, today’s frontier AI models, even ones that process multiple modalities such as text, images, and audio, both take as input and produce discretely quantized tokens. Whether robot actions should follow the same discrete format therefore raises a key question: Are robot actions unique among other AI modalities in that they must be predicted as continuous values, or can discrete action representations compete with, or even outperform, their continuous counterparts?

sections.heading: 1.1 Contributions
sections.text: In this work, we undertake a systematic comparison between the performance of continuous and discrete action parameterizations for both single-task robot policies and multi-task vision-language-action (VLA) models. In short, we show that discrete action parametrization can be competitive with, and even uniformly outperform, continuous action prediction , provided that correct design decisions are made. These findings provide a deeper understanding of the performance of recent discrete diffusion/flow VLA policies ( Liang et al., 2026b ; Wen et al., 2025b ; Chen et al., 2026a ) . In greater detail, we consider parametrizations of the action head , or part of a robot model responsible for action prediction. Our comparison builds on classical supervised control and imitation learning ( Pomerleau, 1988 ; Ross et al., 2011 ; Osa et al., 2018 ) . We focus our study on 4 representative parametrizations: (1) continuous regression (CR), which predicts continuous-valued actions in a single forward pass and is trained with a regression objective ( Bojarski et al., 2016 ; Kim et al., 2025 ) (2) continuous flow (CF), which generates continuous actions using flow matching, a family applied to robot control and motion planning ( Hu et al., 2024 ; Chisari et al., 2024 ; Black et al., 2025 ; Zhang et al., 2024 ; Nguyen et al., 2025 ) (3) discrete regression (DR), which predicts a quantized action via cross-entropy classification ( Brohan et al., 2022 ) and (4) discrete flow (DF), which predicts quantized actions in multiple steps via the discrete flow matching objective ( Gat et al., 2024 ) . Hybrid methods such as Behavior Transformer ( Shafiullah et al., 2022 ) combine discrete action-bin prediction with a continuous offset; in contrast, we study purely discrete and continuous action heads separately to isolate the effect of action representation. Recent work compares regression and flow policies under architecture-matched settings ( Pan et al., 2026 ) . We evaluate these parametrizations from single-task policies on RoboMimic ( Mandlekar et al., 2021 ) to multi-task VLA-scale policies using RoboCasa ( Nasiriany et al., 2026 ) , DROID ( Khazatsky et al., 2024 ) , and LIBERO ( Liu et al., 2023 ) , as well as real-world robot experiments. All are evaluated using closed-loop task success, action prediction accuracy, and within-chunk temporal variation. We identify 3 key findings that upend prior beliefs about the relative performance of discrete and continuous action modalities, challenging the prevailing view that precise robot control requires predicting continuous action prediction: • Finding 1: Control Precision Contrary to prior belief, discrete action parametrizations, even discrete regression (DR) with the simplest bin discretization, can exhibit greater control precision than their continuous counterparts, despite the possibly lossy quantization of actions! We support this claim in both sim and real settings in Section 3 . We show that this arises from greater policy reactivity, both to the action-chunk time index and the conditioning observation. • Finding 2: Iterative Refinement and Guidance Mitigate Factorization Error ( Section 4 ). Independently predicted tokens can combine incompatible choices across time and action dimensions, even when individual token distributions are accurate. DF solves this by iterative computation, while classifier-free guidance reduces ambiguity by changing token preferences. Both improve control significantly, supporting joint consistency as main explanation for their gains. In the RoboCasa comparison, guidance raises DR success from 27.1% to 49.2%, approaching DF’s 53.9% and CF’s 52.7%, largely ahead of CR’s 38.8%. • Finding 3: Explicit Geometry and Structured Tokenization Provide Limited Additional Gains ( Section 5 ). Encoding action distances or using alternative tokenizers improves some configurations, but none exceeds our best DF result with uniform bins and the standard mixture path. Adjacent bins also acquire similar output embeddings, suggesting that discrete heads can learn local geometry without encoding it explicitly. We discuss related work in Appendix A .

sections.heading: 3 Discrete Action Prediction Can Match Continuous Parametrizations
sections.text: In this section, we demonstrate that discrete action prediction matches, and often outperforms continuous action prediction across both flow and regression policies. To evaluate performance, and refute possible precision loss under action discretization, we measure (1) task success rate under closed-loop deployment, and (2) mean ℓ 2 \ell_{2} action prediction error on held-out validation data ( Section B.1 ).

sections.heading: Evaluation Protocol.
sections.text: To demonstrate that our findings are broadly applicable, we consider a wide breadth of tasks; we defer further implementation details to Appendix B . • Single-Task Imitation Learning. To test whether discrete policies’ advantages depend on pretrained VLM, we train separate policies from scratch, without a pretrained VLM backbone, on the Can, Square, Tool Hang and Transport tasks in the RoboMimic suite ( Mandlekar et al., 2021 ) . In particular Tool Hang and Transport are representative of tasks that demand high control precision. Architectures and training settings are in Section C.6.1 . • VLA Scale Tasks in sim. We post-train the PaliGemma Beyer et al. (2024) VLM, used by the � \pi -series models Black et al. (2025) ; Physical Intelligence and others (2025) , with new action heads corresponding to each action head parametrization. As representatives of VLA training, we train on one mixture of eight sources: six RoboCasa365 datasets ( Nasiriany et al., 2024 ; Nasiriany et al., 2026 ) , including MimicGen-generated demonstrations ( Mandlekar et al., 2023 ) , LIBERO-plus ( Fei et al., 2025 ) , and DROID ( Khazatsky et al., 2024 ) . We measure closed-loop success on RoboCasa and LIBERO ( Liu et al., 2023 ) ; DROID has no simulator and serves the offline diagnostics. Evaluations on RoboCasa are grouped into 3 categories: atomic-seen and composite-seen consisting of atomic and composite tasks, respectively, that are contained in the training data; and composite-unseen, consisting of tasks that require compositions of in-distribution atomic-seen, but in novel combinations. The training mixture is in Section B.4 , the architecture in Section C.6.2 , and the evaluation protocol in Section B.3 . • Real World VLA tasks . We used the same backbone and action head setting in sim but trained on different real datasets and SFT on three tasks: throw bottles into bins, open pen caps, and turn mug up. sections.heading: Results.
sections.text: We depict the closed-loop performance of all four policy parametrizations : CR, CF, DR, DF in Fig. 1 (b,c). We see two surprising findings: (i) across VLA and single-task, from-scratch training, discrete flow is competitive with, and often slightly surpasses, continuous flow. More surprisingly, (ii) discrete regression consistently outperforms continuous regression. Section D.3 reports results with other backbone settings, and Section D.2 with other action parameterizations. The fact that discrete regression outperforms its continuous counterpart, even on single-task from scratch training, debunks two widely held hypotheses: (a) that precision is a fundamental bottleneck to discrete policies ( Shafiullah et al., 2022 ) ; (b) that discrete policies are only beneficial in VLA settings, where it has been hypothesized, that discrete predictions are more compatible with token-based VLM backbones ( Brohan et al., 2023 ; Driess et al., 2025 ) . As further evidence that discrete policies are not fundamentally limited by precision, we present their end-effector reconstruction error in Fig. 2 , showing that discrete policies remain competitive (and in some cases slightly outperforms) their continuous counterparts. In fact, in Fig. 2 , we show that discrete flow policies in particular enjoy lower end-effector error early on in the action chunk generation and along the finer motion regime, suggesting the potential for greater precision when actions are discrete.

To identify differences that persist between DF and CF, Fig. 2 (b,c) reveal that discrete policies better fit other subtle variations: in (b), we see that discrete modalities offer more response to smaller degrees of EEF movement, especially the 0–5 mm range (note the logarithmic plot scale); in (c) we see that DF in particular fits actions earlier in the chunk more accurately, which require smaller relative motion. We hypothesize that continuous objectives underweight/over-smooth small action differences compared to categorical prediction. In Section H.1 , we corroborate these hypotheses in controlled studies of fitting synthetic functions with varying levels of smoothness.

sections.heading: DR/DF Exhibit Greater State Responsiveness than CR/CF.
sections.text: Beyond temporal variation within a chunk, we examine state responsiveness : how much the predicted chunk changes when the observation changes along a real trajectory, formally ∂ � ∂ o \frac{\partial\pi}{\partial o} , compared with the expert’s change ( Section E.3.2 ). Fig. 3 shows that both continuous heads produce smaller changes in their mean predicted chunks than their discrete counterparts, underestimating expert change magnitudes on held-out data. DR tracks the expert response most closely, while DF remains closer than CF at every tested state displacement. On the other hand, additional diagnostics in Section E.3 also show that CF stays closer to nearby training actions than DF, 2 2 2 Closeness to training actions is measured by an expert-calibrated excess distance to the nearest training chunks. This measure, the disturbance protocol, and the sampling baselines are defined in Section E.4 . corroborating findings from Pan et al. (2026) . These results suggest that stronger adherence to the training data may come at the cost of responsiveness. DF may offer a better balance, retaining the disturbance stability of flow heads, a small change in the predicted distribution after a small simulator disturbance ( Section E.3.1 ), while responding more closely to expert changes. Takeaway 1: Discrete policies generally match or exceed the control performance of their continuous counterparts across the evaluated testbeds. They obtain stronger performance in both VLA and from-scratch settings. These gains arise from better capturing variation across within-chunk time steps and conditioning observations, rather than outright reconstruction error.

sections.heading: 4 Factorization Error and Iterative Computation in Discrete Policies
sections.text: Thus far, Section 3 establishes that discrete regression (DR) outperforms continuous regression (CR), in part due to better capturing temporal variation, subtle action changes, and response to the input variables. In this section, we show that the greater temporal reactivity observed in DR comes at the cost of action inconsistency, or what we call factorization error (Finding A), harming policy performance. We then identify that the key interventions which enhance performance—applying classifier-free-guidance (Finding B) and introducing iterative computation by moving to discrete flow (Finding C) —correct this inconsistency via complementary mechanisms described below.

sections.heading: Factorization Error in Discrete Policies.
sections.text: DR predicts a categorical distribution for each action token, giving the factorized distribution p � ​ ( 𝐳 ∣ o ) = ∏ j p � , j ​ ( z j ∣ o ) p_{\theta}(\mathbf{z}\mid o)=\prod_{j}p_{\theta,j}(z_{j}\mid o) . When an observation admits several plausible behaviors, different token distributions can assign probability to alternatives behaviors independently. These independent choices can combine incompatible alternatives across time steps and action dimensions. We refer to this failure to preserve dependencies between token choices as factorization error . This may occur even when every token marginal is learned correctly, because the product of the marginals need not recover the joint distribution of demonstrated chunks.

sections.heading: Evaluation Protocol for Factorization Error.
sections.text: To isolate token ambiguity as a potential source of incompatible action tokens, we vary (i) the number of function evaluations (NFE), that is, the number of refinement steps N N in DF, comparing to DR as a baseline, and (ii) the guidance weight � \lambda of classifier-free guidance (CFG, Section 2 ). Note that greater NFE provides more opportunity for self-correction, whereas greater CFG “sharpens” the generated action distribution. Due to space constraints, policy performance under varying CFG/NFE is reported in Section F.3 ; in short, performance improves with NFE and an appropriate guidance weight. Here, we focus on two metrics, deferring precise details to Section F.1 : 1. Mode-mixture : we identify distributions with at least two “incompatible” modes in the same action chunk. We report the mean count of such modes within one chunk across NFE Fig. 4 (a, top) and across guidance weights Fig. 4 (b). 2. Translation Quantiles . Next, we measure the diversity of actions generated across repeated policy samples from the same observation. This lets us test (and ultimately rule out) an alternative hypothesis that DF improves performance over DR by better capturing multimodality. Specifically, we measure the central-90% interval width W 90 = Q 0.95 − Q 0.05 W_{90}=Q_{0.95}-Q_{0.05} for each of the three translation coordinates per time step, and take the Euclidean norm of the 3 per-axis widths. We plot the norm of median widths against NFE in Fig. 4 (a, bottom) and guidance weight in Fig. 4 (c). Lastly, Fig. 4 (d) qualitatively visualizes action diversity. sections.heading: Finding A: Factorization Error Across Horizon and Coordinates Can Limit DR.
sections.text: In Fig. 4 (a), we show that DR suffers from more mode-mixture than DF, even worse at zero CFG. As further evidence, Fig. 5 illustrates the mechanism in the simple Push-T environment. Here, DR assigns probability to separated movement alternatives, and their relative mass changes across the prediction horizon. Section F.4 presents the analogous ambiguity in RoboCasa. These examples confirm the quantitative findings in Fig. 4 , illustrating how factorized decoding can introduce spurious temporal variation, even when individual token predictions capture plausible alternatives.

sections.heading: Finding B: Classifier-Free Guidance Reduces Ambiguity and Makes DR Competitive with DF.
sections.text: As further evidence of the presence of factorization error, we observe that increasing guidance from CFG 0 to CFG 2 raises pooled RoboCasa success from 27.1% to 49.2% ( Section F.3.2 ). This coincides with drastic reduction in the mean-width of the confidence intervals ( Fig. 4 (c)), which is consistent with reductions in spurious temporal variation. As noted above, guidance is known to “sharpen” the resulting generated distribution ( Ho and Salimans, 2022 ; Karras et al., 2024 ) , and thus is likely to be resolving mode ambiguity. Moreover, Fig. 4 (c,d) shows that CFG reduces coverage of plausible ground-truth EEF positions, suggesting that performance advantages from CFG primarily reflect reduced factorization error rather than improved prediction accuracy. Across sources, CFG almost never improves EEF error by more than 1 mm ( Section E.2 ).

sections.heading: Finding C: Iterative Computation Aids Discrete Policies via Reducing Factorization Error.
sections.text: While CFG guidance is a partial-yet-imperfect remedy of factorization error, Here we conclude we show that iterative computation, as in DF, reduces factorization error further. To support this claim, we find that DF reduces the number of inconsistent-mode predictions per chunk by a factor of 5.28 relative to DR, bringing the average below one at NFE ≥ 10 \geq 10 ( Fig. 4 (a,top)). This coincides with a 4.7-point increase in RoboCasa success ( Section F.3 ). These suggest that iterative computation makes discrete action predictions more cohesive than guidance alone. We note that, for continuous action predictions, the benefits of iterative computation are somewhat opposite , combating over-smoothing ( Fig. 2 ) and policy under-reactivity ( Fig. 5 ). The high level role of iterative computation, however, is the same, in that it performs self-correction on policy actions ( Pan et al., 2026 ) . sections.heading: Does action diversity explain the performance of DF? (Likely not)
sections.text: Despite exhibiting low factorization error, DF exhibits greater action diversity than DR, as shown in all Fig. 4 plots. However, this is unlikely to explain its greater performance. CFG 2 notably reduces DF action diversity, and reduces action diversity in CF and DR considerably more; yet in all three, performance increases, most notably in DR (see Section F.3 ). Moreover, although performance improves up to NFE = 10 =10 , action diversity remains relatively constant ( Fig. 4 (a,bottom) and Fig. 12 ). These findings suggest that preservation of full action diversity in the policy is not essential for task success.

sections.heading: Can temporal autoregression resolve factorization error?
sections.text: Temporal autoregression provides another way to coordinate action choices across time. We implement a discrete autoregressive (AR) policy that predicts the first action from the observation, then predicts each subsequent action conditioned on the observation and all previously generated actions. Coordinates within each time step are predicted in parallel, requiring 24 sequential predictions for a 24-step chunk. Without CFG, temporal AR achieves 42.8% success on RoboCasa, exceeding DR’s 27.1% but remaining below DF. However, with CFG, the AR slightly trails both DR and DF ( Tab. 1 ). Takeaway 2: We identify factorization error , a form of temporal inconsistency, as the cause of DR’s relative lack of performance compared to CF and DF. Iterative computation in DF yields maximal performance, but with appropriate CFG, DR’s performance is surprising close ; this reveals that iterative computation and distribution sharpening are both effective means for combating factorization errors.

sections.heading: 5 Additional Structure Provides Limited Gains for Discrete Policies
sections.text: Section 4 links the gains from iterative refinement and guidance to reduced ambiguity in discrete action predictions. In this section, we ask can explicit action geometry or structured tokenization further improve on simple categorical prediction with uniform bins? We now consider two mechanism for adding structure: encoding metric distances between action values during the DF corruption process, or changing how action chunks are tokenized.

sections.heading: Explicit Geometry Provides Limited Control Gains.
sections.text: We introduce action geometry in two ways. For DR, distance-based label smoothing assigns target probability to nearby action bins as well as the demonstrated bin, with probability decreasing with distance ( Section C.3 ). We combine this with logit soft-capping to limit confidence. For DF, we replace the uniform-source mixture path in Eq. 2.1 with a metric-induced corruption path q t metric ​ ( 𝐳 t ∣ 𝐳 ) = ∏ j = 1 L exp ⁡ [ − � ​ ( � ​ ( t ) ) ​ d ​ ( z t , j , z j ) ] ∑ b = 1 B exp ⁡ [ − � ​ ( � ​ ( t ) ) ​ d ​ ( b , z j ) ] , d ⁡ ( k , b ) = | k − b | ( B − 1 ) / 2 , q_{t}^{\mathrm{metric}}(\mathbf{z}_{t}\mid\mathbf{z})=\prod_{j=1}^{L}\frac{\exp\!\left[-\beta(\alpha(t))\,d(z_{t,j},z_{j})\right]}{\sum_{b=1}^{B}\exp\!\left[-\beta(\alpha(t))\,d(b,z_{j})\right]},\qquad d(k,b)=\frac{|k-b|}{(B-1)/2}, (5.1) where � \beta is an increasing concentration schedule. As generation progresses, the metric path concentrates corrupted tokens near the clean target, whereas the mixture path keeps all incorrect bins equally likely ( Section G.2 ). Both DF variants retain the clean-token prediction objective in Eq. 2.2 . Thus, label smoothing changes DR’s prediction targets, whereas the metric path changes DF’s corrupted inputs. The schedules, sampling rates, and results of each variant are provided in Section G.2 . The tested DR variant improves RoboCasa success by 2.1 points. The best tested metric-path DF reaches 52.8% pooled success, compared with 53.9% for mixture-path DF. Explicit geometry therefore provides a modest gain for DR but does not improve the best observed DF result.

sections.heading: Structured Tokenizers Do Not Improve over Naive Binning.
sections.text: We next test whether changing the action representation improves control. We evaluate Finite Scalar Quantization(nFSQ) ( Mentzer et al., 2024 ) , residual vector quantization (RVQ) ( Zeghidour et al., 2021 ) , and FAST ( Pertsch et al., 2025 ) , alongside quantile-bin baselines. At their best recorded complete operating points, DF reaches 52.4% RoboCasa SR with nFSQ, 46.2% with FAST, and 38.2% with RVQ ( Section G.1 ). For DR, quantile bins and nFSQ beat the unguided flat-bin baseline (49.8% and 41.6%, against 27.1%). Against guided flat-bin DR (49.2%), quantile bins are only marginally better and nFSQ is lower, so the tokenizer matters mainly when DR runs without guidance. However, none of these exceeds the broader campaign’s best flat-bin DF result of 53.9%. The observed gains limited on DR, and do not raise the best recorded performance.

sections.text: Why does encoding structural information yield little benefit? We hypothesize that discrete policy encode geometry through the embedding vectors associated with the last logit layer. Specifically, each bin b b at coordinate j j associated with a last-layer embedding 𝐛𝐯 j , b \mathbf{bv}_{j,b} . For spatially adjacent bins b , b + 1 b,b+1 , we compute the vector cosine cos ⁡ � j , b := ⟨ 𝐯 j , b , 𝐯 j , b + 1 ⟩ ​ ( ‖ 𝐯 j , b ‖ ​ ‖ 𝐯 j , b + 1 ‖ ) \cos\theta_{j,b}:=\langle\mathbf{v}_{j,b},\mathbf{v}_{j,b+1}\rangle(\|\mathbf{v}_{j,b}\|\|\mathbf{v}_{j,b+1}\|) . Embedding plots, probes, and the selected-checkpoint comparison are provided in Section G.3 . Takeaway 3: Explicit geometry and structured tokenization can improve individual configurations, but neither exceeds the best configuration of DF with uniform masking and flat-bin tokenization. Learned local geometry offers a possible explanations for these limited gains.

sections.heading: 6 Discussion and Future Work
sections.text: We began by asking whether robot actions are fundamentally different from other AI modalities in requiring continuous prediction. Our results challenge this distinction. Although robots operate in a continuous physical world, simple action tokens can support precise control in both simulation and real-world tasks. Their success shows that discrete action prediction is more than a convenient interface to a language model. It is an effective way to learn robot control in its own right. The key difficulty exposed by our experiments is deciding which token choices belong together. Discrete heads readily express action variation, but independent predictions can combine incompatible behaviors. Iterative refinement and guidance help resolve these conflicts while retaining responsiveness. This connects action prediction to a challenge also studied in diffusion language models: accurate token predictions must be coordinated to form a coherent joint output. The need for joint consistency also suggests a different objective for action tokenization. Although the tested reconstruction-based tokenizers do not improve on our best uniform-bin DF result, tokenizers designed to make coupled action choices easier to predict may help reduce factorization error. For example, tokens could jointly encode coherent motion across several time steps. Their value may depend on the prediction head and the number of generation steps available. Finding tokenizations suited to discrete regression, iterative flow, or generation with only a few refinement steps is therefore a promising direction. Such tokenizers should be evaluated by the consistency and control performance of the resulting policies, alongside reconstruction quality. More broadly, these findings support learning action generation within the same token-based framework as perception and reasoning. A natural next step is to test whether sharing representations and prediction machinery across modalities improves co-training and transfer, while preserving the action consistency needed for closed-loop control.These results make a strong case for treating discrete action prediction as a central component of future robot foundation models.

sections.heading: Action representations.
sections.text: Early generalist policies predicted actions as tokens. RT-1 discretizes each action coordinate into 256 uniform bins [ Brohan et al., 2022 ] , RT-2 and OpenVLA reuse such bins as tokens of a pretrained vision-language model [ Brohan et al., 2023 , Kim et al., 2024 ] , and Gato trains one transformer from scratch on text and on actions in 1024 bins [ Reed et al., 2022 ] . The field has since moved to continuous heads, motivated by the precision of continuous outputs and by the ability of diffusion models to represent multimodal action distributions. Diffusion Policy and ACT generate continuous chunks [ Chi et al., 2023 , Zhao et al., 2023 ] , Octo and RDT-1B use a diffusion head or backbone [ Octo Model Team et al., 2024 , Liu et al., 2025 ] , and most recent VLAs attach a diffusion or flow-matching module to a pretrained VLM [ Li et al., 2024a , Black et al., 2025 , Physical Intelligence and others, 2025 , NVIDIA et al., 2025 , Shukor et al., 2025 ] or regress actions directly [ Kim et al., 2025 ] . Methods that keep discrete actions usually add machinery to address a perceived weakness of plain bins. Behavior Transformers add a continuous offset to a discrete cluster to recover precision [ Shafiullah et al., 2022 , Cui et al., 2023 , Lee et al., 2024 ] . FAST, vector and scalar quantization, and B-spline tokenizers compress chunks into shorter token sequences [ Pertsch et al., 2025 , Lee et al., 2024 , Belkhale and Sadigh, 2024 , Wang et al., 2025b , Mete et al., 2024 , Zhou et al., 2025 ] . HybridVLA and knowledge insulation combine a discrete token loss with a continuous action objective in one model [ Liu et al., 2026a , Driess et al., 2025 ] . We ask whether this machinery is needed. Our discrete heads predict plain per-coordinate uniform bins, and Section 5 tests several of these tokenizers.

sections.heading: Comparisons of discrete and continuous heads.
sections.text: The move to continuous heads rests partly on studies that swap the action head within one model and find continuous heads stronger [ Octo Model Team et al., 2024 , Li et al., 2024b , Kim et al., 2025 , Hou et al., 2025 , Wu et al., 2026b , Ye et al., 2026a ] . Octo, RoboVLMs, and OpenVLA-OFT attribute the gap to bin precision. But these studies change the representation together with other choices. The discrete head usually decodes tokens autoregressively, and FAST shows that autoregressive decoding of per-step bins fails at 20 Hz and 50 Hz [ Pertsch et al., 2025 ] . The discrete head is often a linear projection onto the language-model vocabulary while the continuous head is a new MLP [ Li et al., 2024b , Kim et al., 2025 ] , and the discrete baselines in Diffusion Policy and ACT predict one action at a time [ Chi et al., 2023 , Zhao et al., 2023 ] . When all tokens are decoded in one pass, the gap shrinks or reverses. RT-1’s one-pass bins outperform a unimodal Gaussian head [ Brohan et al., 2022 ] , BEAST’s parallel tokens outperform L1 regression on the same B-spline representation [ Zhou et al., 2025 ] , BAKU’s BeT and VQ-BeT heads match an MLP head and match or beat a diffusion head [ Haldar et al., 2024 ] , and Discrete Diffusion VLA reports 94.2% LIBERO success for parallel bins, 81.2% for autoregressive bins, and 94.9% for a continuous diffusion head [ Liang et al., 2026b ] . The evidence is still not one-sided: parallel bins trail L1 regression in OpenVLA-OFT (90.2% vs. 95.3%) [ Kim et al., 2025 ] , and the ranking of heads in Dream-VLA changes with the backbone [ Ye et al., 2025a ] . Separating the representation from the decoding requires varying them independently. Pan et al. [2026] do this for continuous heads, comparing regression and flow under matched architectures. We extend the comparison to discrete heads, crossing continuous and discrete representations with one-pass and iterative generation under one backbone and training recipe.

sections.heading: Discrete diffusion and flow policies.
sections.text: A second line of work keeps discrete actions and replaces autoregressive decoding with iterative parallel decoding. Discrete Diffusion VLA decodes 256-bin action tokens inside the VLM by confidence-ordered unmasking [ Liang et al., 2026b ] . Some VLAs build on diffusion language models: LLaDA-VLA and MMaDA-VLA start from one [ Wen et al., 2025b , Liu et al., 2026b ] , and Dream-VLA pretrains one on discrete action tokens before fine-tuning a flow head [ Ye et al., 2025a ] . A shared token space also lets one model generate actions together with text and images. dVLA, UD-VLA, and MMaDA-VLA denoise these tokens jointly [ Wen et al., 2025a , Chen et al., 2026a , Liu et al., 2026b ] , and MM-ACT co-trains the three generation tasks [ Liang et al., 2026a ] . Later work targets speed and deployment through block diffusion and caching [ Lee et al., 2026 , Wang et al., 2026b , Song et al., 2026 ] , structured masks [ Yang et al., 2026 ] , inpainting for asynchronous execution [ Wang et al., 2026a ] , and RL fine-tuning [ Wu et al., 2026c ] . The approach also extends to policies trained without a VLM [ He et al., 2024 , Zhuang et al., 2026 ] and to driving [ Li et al., 2026c , Xu et al., 2025 , Dang et al., 2026 ] . Closest to our DF head, DFM-VLA and WAM-Flow use discrete flow matching with a uniform source and a metric-induced path [ Chen et al., 2026b , Xu et al., 2026 ] , and E0 trains a � 0 \pi_{0} -style expert with cross-entropy on Gaussian-noised one-hot bins [ Zhan et al., 2025 ] . This work focuses on building faster and more capable models, and leaves open why iterative decoding helps. Several of these papers find that it beats one-pass decoding in the same model [ Liang et al., 2026b , Lee et al., 2026 , Liang et al., 2026a ] , but fewer than half train a continuous head on the same backbone, none of the manipulation policies applies classifier-free guidance to action tokens, and DFM-VLA and WAM-Flow do not compare the metric path to a uniform-source mixture path with all else fixed. Section 4 attributes the gain of iterative decoding to reduced factorization error and adds guidance, and Section 5 tests metric-induced paths.

sections.heading: Discrete diffusion and flow models.
sections.text: Our DF head builds on discrete diffusion [ Austin et al., 2021 , Hoogeboom et al., 2021 , Campbell et al., 2022 ] , in particular its masked variant [ Lou et al., 2024 , Sahoo et al., 2024 , Shi et al., 2024 , Ou et al., 2025 , Chang et al., 2022 , Chang et al., 2023 ] , which now scales to large language models [ Nie et al., 2025 , Ye et al., 2025b ] , and on discrete flow matching [ Gat et al., 2024 , Campbell et al., 2024 ] . Shaul et al. [2025] extend discrete flow matching to arbitrary paths and propose the metric-induced path tested in Section 5 . Uniform sources and remasking samplers, which let committed tokens change, are related alternatives [ Schiff et al., 2025 , Sahoo et al., 2025 , Deng et al., 2026 , Wang et al., 2025a , Zhao et al., 2025 ] . Most relevant to us, few-step sampling in these models suffers the same factorization error as one-pass action heads, because each step predicts positions independently. ReDi and CoDD reduce this error [ Yoo et al., 2025 , Li et al., 2026a ] , and Tang et al. [2026] show that it persists even with an exact denoiser. Section 4 studies the same error for action chunks.

sections.heading: Discretized control and classification losses.
sections.text: Section 3 shows that discrete heads can match continuous ones despite quantization. Work outside imitation learning suggests why precision is rarely the bottleneck. In reinforcement learning, per-dimension action bins work well on continuous-control benchmarks [ Metz et al., 2017 , Tavakoli et al., 2018 , Tang and Agrawal, 2020 , Seyde et al., 2021 , Seyde et al., 2023 , Chebotar et al., 2023 ] , Dactyl uses only 11 bins per coordinate [ OpenAI et al., 2020 ] , and value and reward heads are often trained with cross-entropy over bins [ Bellemare et al., 2017 , Hafner et al., 2025 , Hansen et al., 2024 ] . HL-Gauss, a cross-entropy loss with Gaussian-smoothed bin targets [ Imani and White, 2018 ] , improves the performance and scaling of deep RL [ Farebrother et al., 2024 ] . Analyses attribute such gains to training rather than to modelling the target distribution: easier optimization in supervised regression [ Imani et al., 2026 ] , robustness to noisy targets and better representations in RL [ Farebrother et al., 2024 ] , and different learned features in two-layer networks [ Stewart et al., 2023 ] . MSE also has a known failure mode. It averages distinct modes [ Shafiullah et al., 2022 ] and smooths over discontinuities [ Florence et al., 2021 ] , and in forecasting, models trained with MSE or quantile losses regress toward the mean or median when the context is uncertain, while cross-entropy over bins can settle on a mode [ Yu et al., 2026 ] . For behavior cloning, the regret with quantized actions and a log-loss depends on the quantization error only polynomially in the horizon, given stable dynamics and a probabilistically smooth policy [ Cao and Xie, 2026 ] . Categorical outputs are also standard for other continuous signals such as pixels and audio [ van den Oord et al., 2016b , van den Oord et al., 2016a ] . For VLAs the evidence is mixed: 512 uniform bins are worse than MSE regression on CALVIN and better on Meta-World [ Szot et al., 2024 ] . Our distance-based label smoothing follows soft ordinal targets [ Gao et al., 2017 , Díaz and Marathe, 2019 , Imani and White, 2018 , Chung et al., 2026 ] , and our logit soft-capping follows Gemma 2 [ Gemma Team et al., 2024 ] .

sections.heading: Classifier-free guidance.
sections.text: Section 4 uses classifier-free guidance [ Ho and Salimans, 2022 ] to sharpen discrete action distributions. For categorical outputs, guidance reweights each token’s distribution directly. Muse applies it to token logits [ Chang et al., 2023 ] , later work formalizes it for discrete diffusion and flow [ Nisonoff et al., 2025 , Schiff et al., 2025 , Rojas et al., 2026 ] , and on language-model logits it lowers entropy while also reordering the top tokens [ Sanchez et al., 2024 ] . We apply the Muse rule to each coordinate’s clean-token distribution. In continuous diffusion the effect is less direct. Guided sampling does not sample the tilted distribution [ Chidambaram et al., 2024 , Bradley and Nakkiran, 2025 ] , and in simple mixtures large weights push samples toward the edge of the support [ Chidambaram et al., 2024 ] . Results on continuous robot policies are mixed. Guidance helps CogACT [ Li et al., 2024a ] and gives a small gain for language-conditioned flow VLAs [ Park et al., 2026 ] , but it is slightly worse than plain goal conditioning in BESO [ Reuss et al., 2023 ] , hurts when applied to the observation [ Pearce et al., 2023 ] , and makes the RDT-1B arm unstable [ Liu et al., 2025 ] . � 0.6 ∗ \pi^{*}_{0.6} notes that large weights push actions to the corners of the support and cause aggressive motions [ Physical Intelligence et al., 2025 ] . On discrete action tokens, the closest prior use is policy contrastive decoding over OpenVLA’s tokens [ Wu et al., 2026a ] . In our experiments, guidance raises DR success on RoboCasa from 27.1% to 49.2% ( Section 4 ).

sections.heading: Appendix B Environment Details
sections.text: This section gives the evaluation measures, training recipes, and comparison protocol for the experiments in Sections 3 , 4 and 5 .

sections.heading: Settings.
sections.text: Our evidence spans pretrained vision–language–action policies, evaluated on RoboCasa and LIBERO and diagnosed offline on DROID, and policies trained from scratch on RoboMimic and Push-T. Controlled function fitting uses separate models with a common trunk architecture to predict deterministic targets from a scalar input. These settings let us examine precision in robot policies and study fitting behavior where the target and codec error are known.

sections.heading: Evaluating action quality.
sections.text: We distinguish three measurements. Prediction error compares predicted and demonstrated actions, reporting training fit and held-out error separately. Robot translation errors use millimeters; Push-T uses pixels. Temporal variation , assessed through jerk, describes variation in the commanded trajectory. Task performance measures closed-loop success on RoboCasa, LIBERO, and RoboMimic in Figure 1 . Robot evaluations use 5 evaluation seeds with per-head checkpoints and inference budgets. Synthetic comparisons use 3 initialization seeds. Formal error definitions, benchmark recipes, and the chronology of the synthetic studies are in Appendices B and H .

sections.heading: B.2 From-Scratch Training Experiments
sections.text: Single-task RoboMimic policies are state-based and trained from scratch, without a pretrained vision–language backbone. Their evaluation protocol and records are in Section D.1 .

sections.heading: B.3 VLA-Scale Experiments
sections.text: All VLA-scale policies are trained on one shared data mixture ( Section B.4 ). They share one PaliGemma backbone, action horizon 24, quantile normalization statistics, and seed 7. Actions are relative end-effector commands for a Franka arm: target poses with respect to the end-effector pose at prediction time, with axis-angle rotation. For each head, we evaluate the last five saved checkpoints, at 110k, 120k, 130k, 140k, and 150k training steps, and report the best of the five. Each evaluation uses five seeds; we report the mean success rate over the seeds, and ± \pm denotes the standard deviation over them. Evaluation replans every 24 steps, and every head runs the same evaluation episodes. The backbone, optimizer, and batch size are given in Section C.6.2 .

sections.heading: RoboCasa.
sections.text: RoboCasa [ Nasiriany et al., 2026 ] is a simulated benchmark of household manipulation tasks in kitchen scenes. We run 10 trials per task on three suites: atomic-seen (180 episodes), composite-seen (160), and composite-unseen (160).

sections.heading: LIBERO.
sections.text: LIBERO [ Liu et al., 2023 ] is a simulated benchmark of language-conditioned tabletop manipulation with a Franka arm. Each suite has 10 tasks with 50 human demonstrations per task. We evaluate closed-loop success on two suites. In LIBERO-Object, the tasks share one layout and differ in which object the robot picks and places in a basket. LIBERO-10 (also called LIBERO-Long) has long-horizon tasks that each chain two subtasks across varied objects, layouts, and scenes. The training mixture contains LIBERO-plus demonstrations ( Section B.4 ), and held-out LIBERO-plus episodes are a validation source for the offline diagnostics.

sections.heading: DROID.
sections.text: DROID [ Khazatsky et al., 2024 ] is a real-world Franka teleoperation dataset of 76k trajectories collected across 564 scenes and 86 tasks. It is part of the VLA training mixture. DROID has no simulator, so we do not measure closed-loop success on it. Held-out DROID chunks instead serve as a validation source for the offline diagnostics: the jerk ratio and EEF error in Fig. 2 , the t-SNE in Fig. 4 (d), and the CFG error sweep in Section E.2 .

sections.heading: B.4 VLA Training Data Mixture
sections.text: The VLA-scale policies train on one mixture of eight sources: six RoboCasa365 datasets [ Nasiriany et al., 2026 ] , LIBERO-plus [ Fei et al., 2025 ] , and DROID [ Khazatsky et al., 2024 ] ( Tab. 2 ). All eight share one action space, a 7-dimensional relative end-effector command for a Franka arm: 3D position and axis-angle rotation with respect to the end-effector pose at prediction time, and gripper. One set of quantile normalization statistics covers the whole mixture. We filter frames before sampling. For RoboCasa, we drop the frames in which the robot drives its mobile base and keep the arm-control frames. For DROID, we keep the successful episodes and remove idle segments. LIBERO-plus is used in full. Each source is sampled with weight proportional to the square root of its frame count. The RoboCasa MimicGen source has 116M frames of synthetic demonstrations. To keep it from dominating the mixture, its frame count is capped at DROID’s when we compute the weight. We hold out 2% of the episodes of every source, chosen with a fixed seed. sections.heading: C.6.2 VLA-Scale Architectures
sections.text: All four heads share a PaliGemma-3B backbone [ Beyer et al., 2024 ] : a SigLIP So400m/14 image encoder and a Gemma-2B language model. We initialize it from the � 0 \pi_{0} vision–language weights [ Black et al., 2025 ] and fine-tune it fully. The backbone reads up to three 224 × 224 224\times 224 camera images (256 tokens each) and up to 48 text tokens with bidirectional attention. A resampler with 64 learned queries (2 blocks, width 1536) compresses the final-layer backbone states, together with one proprioception token, into 64 condition tokens. The action head is a separate transformer with 8 blocks, width 1536, 12 attention heads, and MLP width 6144. Each block applies self-attention over the action sequence, cross-attention to the 64 condition tokens, and an MLP. The head does not share attention layers with the backbone. It processes the H = 24 H=24 action chunk as a sequence with one element per action coordinate ( M = 7 M=7 : 3D position change, axis-angle rotation change, and gripper). Continuous heads represent each element as a real value; discrete heads represent it as a token over B B bins. Learned position and coordinate embeddings and Fourier features of the flow time are added to every element. Tab. 5 lists what all heads share, what each representation shares, what differs per head, and the training settings. Bins are uniform over the normalized action range. DF uses a uniform source, and the reported DF policy uses the schedule � ​ ( t ) = t 3 \alpha(t)=t^{3} . The condition is dropped with probability 0.1 and replaced by a learned null condition, which enables CFG at inference ( Section C.5 ). Training settings are listed in Tab. 5 , and the evaluation protocol, including checkpoint selection and seeds, is given in Section B.3 .

sections.heading: E.3 State Responsiveness and Disturbance Stability
sections.text: Question Can a policy stay stable under small disturbances while still responding to real state changes? We measure two properties of how a head’s predictions change with the observation. State responsiveness asks whether the predicted chunk changes as much as the demonstrated chunk when the state changes along a real trajectory. Disturbance stability asks how little the distribution of predicted chunks moves after a small disturbance, compared with the head’s own sampling variation. The two pull against each other: a head that changes little with its input is stable but under-responsive. Flow heads have the highest disturbance stability, and within the flow family DF is more responsive than CF. The state-responsiveness result in Fig. 3 is the lag-4 row of Tab. 10 .

sections.heading: Mode-detection criteria.
sections.text: For each translation-token distribution p j ​ ( b ) p_{j}(b) , we smooth probabilities along the bin axis with a Gaussian kernel of standard deviation two bins, normalized over the available bins at each location. We identify local maxima, including endpoint maxima, in the smoothed distribution. Each bin is assigned to its nearest peak, and each peak’s mass is the sum of the unsmoothed probabilities assigned to it. We retain peaks with at least 10% mass. Two adjacent retained peaks qualify as separated modes if they are at least eight bins apart and the minimum smoothed probability between them is at most 50% of the smaller peak height. Each translation token represents one coordinate at one predicted time step. We call it ambiguous if it has a qualifying pair of modes, and count it once regardless of how many such pairs it has. The mean count averages ambiguous tokens per chunk. The threshold statistic reports the fraction of chunks containing at least k k ambiguous tokens. For DF, detection is performed on each final conditional token prediction before averaging over refinement draws.

sections.heading: H.1 Which Fine Structure Does Categorical Prediction Preserve?
sections.text: The robot experiments raise a simple question: can a model get the broad motion right and still miss the fine detail? Robot data mixes too many factors to answer this, so we use synthetic targets where we control the fine structure directly.

sections.heading: Hypothesis 2: categorical prediction can preserve steep fine structure.
sections.text: Following the multiscale construction of Pan et al. [2026] , each target is a broad sine plus a small fine-scale term. In the first target the fine term is a fast sine. In the second it is a square wave, which jumps between two values and so has no finite Lipschitz constant. CF and DF both predict clean targets. Figure 19 : Precision depends on target structure. Each target pairs original predictions (seed 0) with held-out MSE for all three seeds; marks indicate means and the dashed line indicates the hard-bin codec floor. Prediction axes use the local target range; all errors remain included. CF/DF curves show one draw, while stochastic MSE averages eight per-draw errors. Both fine-term amplitude and shape change between targets.

sections.heading: Smooth fine detail: continuous regression wins.
sections.text: On the smooth target (Figure 19 A), CR’s held-out error is about 250 times lower than DR’s. Both continuous heads go below the codec’s reconstruction floor. That floor limits any output decoded through argmax, but not continuous outputs. The discrete heads stay well above it, so bin resolution alone does not explain their larger error.

sections.heading: Steep fine detail: the ordering reverses.
sections.text: On the square-wave target (Figure 19 B), DR has the lowest held-out error of all heads, with 3.2 times lower MSE and 4.5 times lower MAE than CR. DF also beats both continuous heads, with 31 percent lower error than CF. The prediction panel shows the difference. The regression heads follow the steps but round off the corners, while the categorical heads jump to the next bin right at the edge.

sections.heading: Controls narrow the explanation.
sections.text: Quantized Regression fits the bin centers with squared error. It behaves like CR on both targets, so discrete target values are not what drives DR’s result. CF tracks CR and DF trails DR on both targets, so the reversal shows up with one-pass and iterative prediction alike. That leaves the categorical formulation as a whole: loss, output parameterization, and argmax decoding. One likely reason is argmax itself. The logits can change smoothly while the decoded bin jumps, which lets the model represent sharp transitions.

Abstract Though modern AI models like LLMs predict discrete tokens, today’s robotic foundation models represent actions as continuous vectors. In this paper, we challenge this common consensus by asking if continuous action parametrizations are superior to their discrete counterparts. We conduct an extensive comparison of single-step regression and multi-step flow variants of both continuous and discrete policies in both from-scratch single-task and multi-task VLA training, in both simulation and on real hardware. In all regimes, we find that discrete action prediction, even the most naive, uniform-bin quantization, can match or even outperform continuous-action policies in task success rate. Moreover, we find that the challenge to discrete action policies is not action precision, but rather factorization error introduced by product-distribution predictions across time and action dimensions. We show that, when paired with the correct interventions—iterative computation through discrete flows, or distribution sharpening through classifier-free guidance—discrete flow policies can turn this weakness into a strength, enabling more responsive action changes during a predicted action chunk. Lastly, we show that attempts to explicitly inject geometric information into discrete policies, e.g. through corruption processes that emulate continuous flow matching, do not yield consistent improvements. Taken together, our findings question existing assumptions that robotic action prediction requires distinct design decisions compared to other AI domains, and motivates the possibility of discrete action prediction as a compelling alternative to today’s continuous action parametrizations. Date: October 14, 2026 Website: https://iscoyizj.github.io/discrete-action-website/ 1 Introduction A major goal of modern robot learning is to perform complex and varied tasks to high precision. As a result, the community has devoted significant study to the question of how to parametrize the actions predicted by robotic policies and foundation models, such as vision-language-action models (VLAs) ( Brohan et al., 2023 ; Kim et al., 2024 ; Black et al., 2025 ; NVIDIA et al., 2025 ) and world action models (WAMs) ( Li et al., 2025 ; Ye et al., 2026b ; Kim et al., 2026 ; Li et al., 2026b ) . The common consensus is that robot models should predict continuous-valued actions during deployment, as these are lossless and therefore support high-precision behavior. For example, most of today’s VLAs predict actions using continuous-space generative models, such as flow ( Black et al., 2025 ; Physical Intelligence and others, 2025 ) or diffusion models ( Chi et al., 2023 ) , which are believed to better capture training data diversity whilst enhancing the precision of action predictions. At the same time, modern robot learning is adopting increasingly more features from other AI domains, notably language modeling. These include test-time reasoning ( Wei et al., 2022 ) , on-task self-correction ( Huang et al., 2022 ) , future goal prediction ( Du et al., 2023 ) , and long-term memory ( Wang et al., 2023 ) . In fact, recent work has showcased the possibility that frontier language models can directly control robot embodiments through text generation ( Brohan et al., 2023 ; Kim et al., 2024 ) . Yet, today’s frontier AI models, even ones that process multiple modalities such as text, images, and audio, both take as input and produce discretely quantized tokens. Whether robot actions should follow the same discrete format therefore raises a key question: Are robot actions unique among other AI modalities in that they must be predicted as continuous values, or can discrete action representations compete with, or even outperform, their continuous counterparts? 1.1 Contributions In this work, we undertake a systematic comparison between the performance of continuous and discrete action parameterizations for both single-task robot policies and multi-task vision-language-action (VLA) models. In short, we show that discrete action parametrization can be competitive with, and even uniformly outperform, continuous action prediction , provided that correct design decisions are made. These findings provide a deeper understanding of the performance of recent discrete diffusion/flow VLA policies ( Liang et al., 2026b ; Wen et al., 2025b ; Chen et al., 2026a ) . In greater detail, we consider parametrizations of the action head , or part of a robot model responsible for action prediction. Our comparison builds on classical supervised control and imitation learning ( Pomerleau, 1988 ; Ross et al., 2011 ; Osa et al., 2018 ) . We focus our study on 4 representative parametrizations: (1) continuous regression (CR), which predicts continuous-valued actions in a single forward pass and is trained with a regression objective ( Bojarski et al., 2016 ; Kim et al., 2025 ) (2) continuous flow (CF), which generates continuous actions using flow matching, a family applied to robot control and motion planning ( Hu et al., 2024 ; Chisari et al., 2024 ; Black et al., 2025 ; Zhang et al., 2024 ; Nguyen et al., 2025 ) (3) discrete regression (DR), which predicts a quantized action via cross-entropy classification ( Brohan et al., 2022 ) and (4) discrete flow (DF), which predicts quantized actions in multiple steps via the discrete flow matching objective ( Gat et al., 2024 ) . Hybrid methods such as Behavior Transformer ( Shafiullah et al., 2022 ) combine discrete action-bin prediction with a continuous offset; in contrast, we study purely discrete and continuous action heads separately to isolate the effect of action representation. Recent work compares regression and flow policies under architecture-matched settings ( Pan et al., 2026 ) . We evaluate these parametrizations from single-task policies on RoboMimic ( Mandlekar et al., 2021 ) to multi-task VLA-scale policies using RoboCasa ( Nasiriany et al., 2026 ) , DROID ( Khazatsky et al., 2024 ) , and LIBERO ( Liu et al., 2023 ) , as well as real-world robot experiments. All are evaluated using closed-loop task success, action prediction accuracy, and within-chunk temporal variation. We identify 3 key findings that upend prior beliefs about the relative performance of discrete and continuous action modalities, challenging the prevailing view that precise robot control requires predicting continuous action prediction: • Finding 1: Control Precision Contrary to prior belief, discrete action parametrizations, even discrete regression (DR) with the simplest bin discretization, can exhibit greater control precision than their continuous counterparts, despite the possibly lossy quantization of actions! We support this claim in both sim and real settings in Section 3 . We show that this arises from greater policy reactivity, both to the action-chunk time index and the conditioning observation. • Finding 2: Iterative Refinement and Guidance Mitigate Factorization Error ( Section 4 ). Independently predicted tokens can combine incompatible choices across time and action dimensions, even when individual token distributions are accurate. DF solves this by iterative computation, while classifier-free guidance reduces ambiguity by changing token preferences. Both improve control significantly, supporting joint consistency as main explanation for their gains. In the RoboCasa comparison, guidance raises DR success from 27.1% to 49.2%, approaching DF’s 53.9% and CF’s 52.7%, largely ahead of CR’s 38.8%. • Finding 3: Explicit Geometry and Structured Tokenization Provide Limited Additional Gains ( Section 5 ). Encoding action distances or using alternative tokenizers improves some configurations, but none exceeds our best DF result with uniform bins and the standard mixture path. Adjacent bins also acquire similar output embeddings, suggesting that discrete heads can learn local geometry without encoding it explicitly. In this section, we show that the greater temporal reactivity observed in DR comes at the cost of action inconsistency, or what we call factorization error (Finding A), harming policy performance. We then identify that the key interventions which enhance performance—applying classifier-free-guidance (Finding B) and introducing iterative computation by moving to discrete flow (Finding C) —correct this inconsistency via complementary mechanisms described below. Factorization Error in Discrete Policies. DR predicts a categorical distribution for each action token, giving the factorized distribution p � ​ ( 𝐳 ∣ o ) = ∏ j p � , j ​ ( z j ∣ o ) p_{\theta}(\mathbf{z}\mid o)=\prod_{j}p_{\theta,j}(z_{j}\mid o) . When an observation admits several plausible behaviors, different token distributions can assign probability to alternatives behaviors independently. These independent choices can combine incompatible alternatives across time steps and action dimensions. We refer to this failure to preserve dependencies between token choices as factorization error . This may occur even when every token marginal is learned correctly, because the product of the marginals need not recover the joint distribution of demonstrated chunks. Finding A: Factorization Error Across Horizon and Coordinates Can Limit DR. In Fig. 4 (a), we show that DR suffers from more mode-mixture than DF, even worse at zero CFG. As further evidence, Fig. 5 illustrates the mechanism in the simple Push-T environment. These examples confirm the quantitative findings in Fig. 4 , illustrating how factorized decoding can introduce spurious temporal variation, even when individual token predictions capture plausible alternatives. Finding B: Classifier-Free Guidance Reduces Ambiguity and Makes DR Competitive with DF. As further evidence of the presence of factorization error, we observe that increasing guidance from CFG 0 to CFG 2 raises pooled RoboCasa success from 27.1% to 49.2% ( Section F.3.2 ). This coincides with drastic reduction in the mean-width of the confidence intervals ( Fig. 4 (c)), which is consistent with reductions in spurious temporal variation. As noted above, guidance is known to “sharpen” the resulting generated distribution ( Ho and Salimans, 2022 ; Karras et al., 2024 ) , and thus is likely to be resolving mode ambiguity. Moreover, Fig. 4 (c,d) shows that CFG reduces coverage of plausible ground-truth EEF positions, suggesting that performance advantages from CFG primarily reflect reduced factorization error rather than improved prediction accuracy. Across sources, CFG almost never improves EEF error by more than 1 mm ( Section E.2 ). Finding C: Iterative Computation Aids Discrete Policies via Reducing Factorization Error. While CFG guidance is a partial-yet-imperfect remedy of factorization error, Here we conclude we show that iterative computation, as in DF, reduces factorization error further. To support this claim, we find that DF reduces the number of inconsistent-mode predictions per chunk by a factor of 5.28 relative to DR, bringing the average below one at NFE ≥ 10 \geq 10 ( Fig. 4 (a,top)). This coincides with a 4.7-point increase in RoboCasa success ( Section F.3 ). These suggest that iterative computation makes discrete action predictions more cohesive than guidance alone. We note that, for continuous action predictions, the benefits of iterative computation are somewhat opposite , combating over-smoothing ( Fig. 2 ) and policy under-reactivity ( Fig. 5 ). The high level role of iterative computation, however, is the same, in that it performs self-correction on policy actions ( Pan et al., 2026 ) . Temporal autoregression provides another way to coordinate action choices across time. We implement a discrete autoregressive (AR) policy that predicts the first action from the observation, then predicts each subsequent action conditioned on the observation and all previously generated actions.
